 Future Eagles Fits: Dynamic tight ends to know in the 2027 NFL Draft 
 Our weekly deep dive into the prospects who could eventually find their way to Philadelphia. 
 By Ryan Fowler • 
 Published October 31, 2026 
 BOOKMARKER 
 Share 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to the media on Thursday and was asked about the progress he’s seen from rookie tackle Markel Bell this season.
 Welcome back to Future Eagles Fits , our weekly deep dive into the prospects who could eventually find their way to Philadelphia.
 Every week, we're going inside the tape and looking at prospects through an Eagles-centric lens — breaking down the athletic profile, positional versatility and scheme fit that could ultimately determine whether a player makes sense in Philly. Along the way, we'll examine how prospects are being evaluated across the league as draft boards begin to take shape and conversations are had with representatives across the scouting landscape.
 While the Eagles invested a second-round pick in Eli Stowers this past spring, there are still significant questions surrounding the future of the position in Philadelphia. Dallas Goedert's long-term status remains uncertain with the trade deadline approaching, and beyond the veteran tight end and Stowers, the depth chart doesn't offer many proven options. Johnny Mundt was brought in to be an extension of the offensive line and EJ Jenkins (now in Atlanta) had an opportunity to carve out a role, but there is room to add additional talent.
 The bottom line when it comes to the position as a spot that has continued to evolve over the last decade; you can never have enough matchup weapons, particularly in an offense that can benefit from creating mismatches between the numbers and stressing defenses at multiple levels. Whether it's a dynamic receiving threat who can separate against linebackers or a more complete player who can contribute as an in-line blocker, adding talent to the position should remain a consideration.
 Here are four tight ends to know for the 2027 NFL Draft — one potential Day 1 target, one Day 2 prospect and two Day 3 options, along with a local name to become familiar with.
 Day 1: Trey'Dez Green, LSU | 6'6", 238 lbs (verified measurements) 
 It’ll likely come down to Green and Oregon’s Jamari Johnson as TE1 next spring.

 For the LSU product, if you're looking for a tight end who can create matchup problems at multiple levels of the field, Green is one of the most intriguing offensive prospects in the entire class, regardless of position. A former basketball player with a rare combination of size, length and athleticism, Green brings the type of receiving profile that creative offensive coordinators can have a field day with scheming up touches. At 6-foot-6, Green presents an enormous catch radius, but his game goes beyond simply being a big target. 
 He has the movement skills to separate against linebackers, the body control to adjust to passes outside his frame and the ability to use his size to create advantages against smaller defensive backs. His background on the hardwood shows up particularly at the catch point, where he can high-point the football and use his frame to keep defenders on his hip. After totaling 35 receptions for 443 yards and seven TDs in 2025, he's continued to demonstrate his big-play potential this fall, averaging 14.3 yards per reception in four games (missed weeks 4-7 due to injury). The next step in his development will be improving his consistency as a blocker, as his frame and length give him plenty of upside in that area, but adding play strength and developing his technique will be important if he wants to become a three-down, complete NFL tight end.
 For the Eagles, Green would offer a different dimension to what they've already invested in with Stowers. While Stowers is an athletic flex weapon who can create mismatches through alignment versatility, Green brings a similarly intriguing receiving profile with even more size and catch-point advantages. Imagine an offense with both players on the field (12 personnel), forcing defenses to account for two extremely athletic tight ends who can stress the middle of the field in different ways.
 Day 2: Luke Reynolds, Virginia Tech | 6'4", 244 lbs (verified measurements) 
 A former five-star recruit and Penn State transfer, Reynolds has established himself as one of the more productive tight ends in college football. After combining for 35 receptions over two seasons at Penn State, he's taken a significant step forward this fall with the Hokies evolving into a featured part of their passing game. Through eight weeks, Reynolds has hauled in 50 catches for 499 yards and six TDs, showcasing the receiving ability that made him such a highly regarded recruit coming out of high school.
 On tape, Reynolds offers a nice combination of size, athleticism and reliable hands. He's comfortable working underneath, finding space against zone coverage and giving his quarterback a dependable target when plays break down. His ability to work across the formation and create opportunities after the catch makes him an appealing option in a modern passing offense, and he’s also shown a willingness and ability to contribute as a blocker, including working from a flex alignment and engaging defenders on the perimeter. 
 While he doesn't necessarily possess the rare catch radius or explosive mismatch ability that Green brings to the table, Reynolds offers a more balanced profile with the potential to contribute in multiple areas. Continuing to expand his route tree and improving his ability to create separation against NFL-caliber defenders will be important next steps.
 For the Philly, Reynolds would give them another versatile option who could complement Stowers rather than simply duplicate his skill set. His ability to work underneath, contribute in the blocking game and provide a reliable receiving presence could make him an interesting addition to a position group that needs more overall depth. With the way Virginia Tech utilizes him, it provides a good opportunity to evaluate how he can handle an expanded role and whether that production translates against different levels of competition.
 Day 3: Jelani Thurman, North Carolina | 6'5", 249 lbs (verified measurements) 
 An Ohio State transfer, get to know Thurman’s name as he’s a player teams have circled to see during the All-Star circuit (Shrine/Senior Bowl). After spending three seasons with the Buckeyes, where opportunities in a crowded tight end room were limited, he's found a much larger role with the Tar Heels and has quickly become one of their most productive offensive weapons with 52 targets in seven games.
 On tape, Thurman offers an impressive combination of size and athleticism for the position. He's explosive off the line of scrimmage, can threaten defenses vertically and has the movement skills to create separation against linebackers/safeties when working across the formation.
 For the Eagles, Thurman would be an interesting developmental addition with the athletic profile to complement Stowers. His size gives him a different physical presence than some of the smaller move tight ends in the class, while his ability to create mismatches in the passing game offers intriguing upside. If he continues to build on his early-season success, and has a nice pre-draft process, he could sneak into the late Day 2 conversation. 
 Day 3: Terrance Carter Jr., Texas Tech | 6'2", 242 lbs (verified measurements) 
 Carter is a name teams have had circled for multiple years. Following a productive 2025 season in which he caught 55 passes for 624 yards with five TDs, Carter had established himself as one of the more intriguing receiving tight ends in the country and would have been drafted had he declared. Instead, he opted to return to Lubbock for another year.
 Unlike some of the bigger, traditional tight ends in the class, Carter's appeal centers around his ability to create with the football in his hands. He's a natural athlete who can make defenders miss in space, generate yards after the catch and take advantage of opportunities when moved around the formation. His experience lining up both in the slot and in a traditional tight end alignment gives him some versatility, while his ability to operate as an H-back or be utilized on the move adds another dimension to his game. His route-running is still an area that can improve, and his blocking technique and play strength need work, but he won’t be a traditional in-line tight end who is asked to seal edge rushers.
 For the Eagles, Carter would offer another movable piece alongside Stowers who could create opportunities through formation versatility and designed touches. The Eagles don't necessarily need another tight end who brings the exact same skill set as their second-round investment, but finding different ways to create mismatches with multiple athletic options is certainly appealing. While 2026 has seen his production dip so far (166 yards in five starts), Carter's previous numbers provide a clear evaluation to teams of the threat he could be when given the necessary volume.
 Honorable Mention: Peter Clarke, Temple | 6'5", 263 lbs (verified measurements) 
 A local name worth keeping an eye on, Clarke offers an interesting combination of size, receiving ability and blocking upside out of Temple. An outstanding story as a native of England, Clarke has continued to develop since arriving in the United States through the NFL Academy, becoming the focal point of the Owls' offense. 
 A preseason All-American and a John Mackey Award (Top TE in College Football) watch list honoree, through seven games, Clarke has recorded 18 receptions for 272 yards and two TDs, including a five-catch, 127-yard performance against Charlotte in his most recent start and six catches on seven targets against Penn State earlier in the year.
 For the Eagles, Clarke is a prospect who makes sense as a potential late-round developmental option, particularly given the proximity to Philly (Temple plays their home games at the Linc) which allows the team to get their eyes on him as much as they seem fit. He offers a different profile than Stowers and some of the aforementioned names above, with the size to contribute as an in-line tight end while still possessing enough receiving ability to work into the perimeter.
